content:
Searching for a supervisor's email — sometimes even a specific one, like an IBEC group leader's — almost always means the same thing: you have found the group and the papers, and the last step is the human one. The good news: university email addresses are public by design. Here is every free route that works, in the order worth trying.

The 8 free methods that work

  1. The staff/directory page — every university maintains one. Search site:*.edu [name] or the institute's own People search; institute sites (e.g. ibecbarcelona.eu, mpi institutes, .ac.uk departmental pages) all list group leaders with contact details.
  2. The corresponding author footer — the paper that made you want to work with them has an asterisked author with an email in the header or first footnote. That address is current by definition.
  3. The lab's Team/People page — group websites list the PI and often the whole team; the PI's mailto is nearly always on it.
  4. The departmental administrator — search '[department] postgraduate administrator' and ask whether they can forward a short message; administrators route these daily and it signals good manners.
  5. ORCID — orcid.org profiles link institutional pages and sometimes direct emails.
  6. Google Scholar profile — the 'Homepage' link on a Scholar profile usually lands on the personal page with contact info.
  7. ResearchGate — a message request there is slower than email but works when the address is hidden.
  8. The institutional pattern — as a last resort, most universities use predictable formats (f.last@university.edu); verify by checking a colleague's published address before sending.

What to avoid: scraped email lists, paid 'professor databases' and bulk sending. One personalised message beats thirty generic ones, and departments talk.

The 120-word first-contact message

Professors answer short, specific, low-effort-to-read messages. Structure:

  1. Subject: Prospective PhD student — [your topic] (Autumn 2027)
  2. Sentence 1: who you are (degree, university, one credential).
  3. Sentence 2: the specific paper or project of theirs you read, and the precise connection to your interests — not 'I admire your work'.
  4. Sentence 3: what you bring (method, result, publication).
  5. Sentence 4: one clear question: are you taking students for [intake], and is funded supervision possible?
  6. Attach: 1–2 page academic CV. Nothing else.

Our seven supervisor email templates give you the wording for every scenario — cold contact, advertised project, referral — and the follow-up guide covers the silence that follows 70% of first emails.

When you need a reference letter email instead

The same lookup skills apply when asking a professor for a recommendation: find the right address, keep it short, attach your CV, transcript and the call text, and give a clear deadline. Our reference-request templates handle the wording.

Etiquette that decides whether you get a reply

  • One professor, one email — emailing a whole department in one day gets noticed for the wrong reason
  • Wait 7–10 days before one polite follow-up; silence after that is an answer
  • Academic seasons matter — August and late December are dead zones; early autumn is the best window for the following year's intake
  • Address them correctly — Dr/Professor by actual title; getting it wrong is the fastest delete

faqs.question: How do I find a professor's email for a PhD application?
faqs.answer: Start with the university's staff or People directory, then the corresponding-author email on their recent paper, then the lab's team page. If none work, email the departmental postgraduate administrator and ask them to forward your message — all four routes are free and public.

faqs.question: Is it OK to email a PhD supervisor directly?
faqs.answer: Yes — direct, short emails are exactly how most supervisor relationships start, especially for self-arranged and rolling European PhDs. Keep it under 150 words, reference one specific paper or project, attach a 1–2 page academic CV, and ask one clear question about taking students.

faqs.question: What should I write when first emailing a supervisor?
faqs.answer: Four sentences: who you are; the specific paper of theirs you read and why it connects to your work; what you bring (method or result); and whether they are taking PhD students for your target intake, with funded supervision possible. Our supervisor email templates give full wording for cold contact, advertised projects and referrals.

faqs.question: What if the supervisor doesn't reply to my email?
faqs.answer: Wait 7–10 days and send one short, polite follow-up in the same thread. After a second silence, move on — professors receive dozens of these emails and silence usually means no capacity, not a judgement on you. Our follow-up guide covers the timing and the exact wording.

faqs.question: Can I ask the department administrator for a supervisor's email?
faqs.answer: Yes, and it is often the fastest professional route. Search for the department's postgraduate or research administrator, write two sentences about who you are and which group you want to reach, and ask whether they can forward your enquiry or confirm the correct contact.
